The Secret of Secrets: Langdon goes to Prague to hear Katherine Solomon lecture, and then she vanishes along with her manuscript on consciousness.
Under the Eagle: AD 42: Cato, a palace slave turned raw recruit, joins the Second Legion on the Rhine under the hard-drinking centurion Macro, just as Rome sets its sights on Britain. The first of a long, muddy march of books.
Eindeloos bewustzijn: een wetenschappeli: A Dutch cardiologist studies heart patients who were clinically dead for minutes, then came back describing what they saw. Pim van Lommel asks what that means for consciousness, which is one of the subjects Vincent reads about most.
Nexus: A Brief History of Information Ne: Harari follows information from stories and holy books through bureaucracies and newspapers up to AI, arguing that more information has never simply meant more truth.
The Pillars of the Earth: In twelfth-century England a builder called Tom dreams of raising a cathedral, and the town of Kingsbridge grows up around the decades of mud, scaffolding and scheming it takes. One of his all-time favourites.
The City and Its Uncertain Walls: A man remembers a walled town where a girl reads old dreams in a library, and years later he ends up running a small library in the Japanese mountains. Murakami, wells and shadows included.
Not Till We Are Lost: Bob has copied himself so often that the copies have drifted into strangers, scattered across dozens of star systems and not all on speaking terms. Book five of a series he keeps coming back to.
Dune: A noble family takes over a desert planet whose sand holds the most precious spice in the universe, and their son ends up among the desert’s own people. He plays Dune: Imperium, the board game, too.
Imminent: Inside the Pentagon's Hunt for: Luis Elizondo, who ran a little-known Pentagon programme studying unidentified craft, tells what he says he saw from the inside and why he quit in 2017. One for the UFO shelf, which is a long one.
The Player of Games: Gurgeh, the Culture’s finest game-player and bored stiff with it, is sent to a distant empire where one fiendishly complicated game decides who rules. A book for anyone who has lost an evening to Root or Dune: Imperium.
The Narrow Road Between Desires: One day in the life of Bast, Kvothe’s strange apprentice, as he bargains and trades favours around the village while the Waystone Inn sits quiet. It’s the most anyone has heard from the Kingkiller world in years.
A Brief History of Intelligence: Evoluti: The brain told as five big leaps, from worms learning to steer to apes guessing what others think, with today’s AI held up against each one. Brains and AI side by side, which is more or less what he studied at Utrecht.
Cloud Atlas: Six stories, from a nineteenth-century sea voyage to a far-off future, each nested inside the next like Russian dolls, with a birthmark and a few echoes running through them all.
Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of th: Two stories in alternating chapters: a data encryptor in a neon Tokyo running from people who want what’s in his head, and a quiet walled Town where a newcomer reads old dreams from unicorn skulls.
Killing Commendatore: A portrait painter whose marriage has just ended moves into a famous old artist’s house in the mountains, finds a hidden painting in the attic, and hears a bell ringing at night in the woods.
My Big TOE: Awakening: Book 1 of a Trilo: A NASA physicist who spent years doing out-of-body research with Robert Monroe sets out a theory of everything in which consciousness comes first and our physical world is something like a simulation it runs.
The Coming Wave: Technology, Power, and: A DeepMind co-founder on why AI and synthetic biology will be very hard to keep in the box, and what it might take to try anyway.
Elon Musk: Walter Isaacson followed Musk around for two years, through rockets, electric cars and the Twitter takeover, and wrote down what he saw.
Bob de straatkat: The true story of James Bowen, a London busker getting clean, and the injured ginger tom who adopted him and rode about town on his shoulders. Charlie does the shoulder thing too, only claws out and while Vincent’s coding.
The Song of Achilles: The Iliad told by Patroclus, from an awkward boyhood at the court of Peleus to the long years at Troy beside Achilles, the friend he loves. Gods, a centaur tutor and a war whose ending everyone already knows.
The Travelling Cat Chronicles: Satoru and his cat Nana drive across Japan visiting old friends, looking for someone to take Nana in, and much of it is told by Nana himself. With Charlie and George at home, he knows the cat’s side of things.
What's Our Problem?: A Self-Help Book fo: Tim Urban and his stick figures take on why public debate has gone so tribal, sorting thinking into the higher mind and the primitive one rather than left and right.
Sekret Machines: Gods: Volume 1 of Gods: The guitarist from Blink-182 teams up with an occult historian to argue that something hidden, UFOs included, has steered human history, citing sources they call “the Advisors”.
The Diamond Age: Or, a Young Lady's Illu: In a nanotech future of neo-Victorian enclaves, a poor girl in Shanghai ends up with a stolen interactive book meant to raise an aristocrat’s granddaughter, and it starts teaching her to think for herself.
The Science of Enlightenment: Teachings: Shinzen Young, an American who trained as a monk in Japan, treats meditation almost as a science: concentration, sensory clarity and equanimity, with techniques you can test on yourself.
Dimensions: A Casebook of Alien Contact: Vallée lines up modern UFO encounters next to centuries of fairy lore, angels and folk tales, and argues they might be the same phenomenon wearing whatever clothes each age expects.
Project Hail Mary: A man wakes up alone on a spaceship with no memory of who he is, only that the sun is dimming and he may be Earth’s last hope. Then he gets company. One of his favourites.
Heaven's River: A Bob goes missing, and the search leads to an alien-built river world, one endless waterway wrapped round a star, where otter-like locals paddle about in boats. He has a wild-water river of his own, out on the island.
All These Worlds: The third Bobiverse book: the many copies of Bob, a software engineer turned starship, are spread across new colonies while the planet-stripping Others come closer.
The Alchemist: An Andalusian shepherd boy dreams of treasure by the Pyramids, sells his flock and sets off across the desert, meeting an old king, a crystal merchant and an alchemist on the way.
Infinite Awareness: The Awakening of a S: A neuroscientist who spent her career assuming the brain makes the mind has a meditation experience that unsettles her, and goes looking at the research on near-death experiences, out-of-body experiences and consciousness beyond the brain.
For We Are Many: Bob, a software developer uploaded into a space probe, keeps copying himself, and the copies are now evacuating Earth, watching over a stone-age alien race and running into something much bigger.
We Are Legion (We Are Bob): Bob, a software developer, sells his company, gets his head frozen, and wakes up a century later as the computer mind of a self-copying space probe. The start of one of his favourite series.
De jacht op het verloren schaap: A Wild Sheep Chase in Dutch: an adman in Tokyo is sent to find one particular sheep with a star on its back, and ends up somewhere cold in the mountains of Hokkaido. A sheep book on a sheep’s island.
Orakel: One foggy winter morning two teenagers find an eighteenth-century sailing ship lying in a Dutch bulb field, and when one of them climbs aboard, she vanishes. Robert Grim, the occult investigator from Hex, is called in.
Ultimate Journey: The third of Robert Monroe’s books about leaving his body, where his night-time travels take him past the familiar and out towards what he thinks comes after death. Required reading for anyone who reads about out-of-body experiences.
Far Journeys (Journeys Trilogy): Monroe’s second book, written after years of leaving his body at will: stranger trips further out, the beings he calls the Inspecs, and the research institute he built in Virginia to teach others to do it.
The Wedge: Evolution, Consciousness, Str: Scott Carney, who earlier wrote about Wim Hof, goes looking for the gap between a stress and our reaction to it, trying ice baths, breathwork, psychedelics and sweat lodges along the way.
Adventures Beyond the Body: How to Exper: William Buhlman mixes his own out-of-body accounts with practical techniques for trying it yourself, from relaxation routines to things to focus on as you drift off. Part of his long run of reading on the subject.
Spoken van Sonsbeek: A Dutch post-apocalyptic novel set over seven days in a ruined Arnhem, where a small band of survivors scavenges for food around Sonsbeek and fights off something rather like zombies. His home town falling apart, written by a friend who used to live by Park Angerenstein too.
De waarheid over de zaak Harry Quebert: A young novelist with writer’s block goes to help his old mentor, who’s been arrested after the body of a girl missing since 1975 turns up in his garden. Twist after twist.
Journeys Out of the Body: The Classic Wo: In the late 1950s a Virginia radio businessman starts feeling strange vibrations at night and finds himself floating above his own bed. His careful notes on what came next started a whole field. He read the sequel a few months later.
The Storyteller: Tales of Life and Music: Dave Grohl tells his life as a string of stories: a Virginia kid with a guitar, drumming for Nirvana, then starting the Foo Fighters, plus a fair bit about being a dad.
Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close: Nine-year-old Oskar loses his father on 9/11, finds a key in his wardrobe and sets off across New York to find the lock it fits, talking to every stranger named Black on the way.
Breath: The New Science of a Lost Art: James Nestor plugs his nose for ten days in a Stanford experiment, then goes looking for what we’ve forgotten about breathing, from nose-breathing and free divers to very old yogic techniques.
De nieuwe wereldorde: Rob de Wijk argues that China is quietly taking over the lead in the world, through technology, trade and patience, while the West is busy with itself.
A Fire Within: The second Sekret Machines novel, co-written by the Blink-182 frontman: lights over Nevada, a pilot, a journalist and a heiress uncovering a cover-up, and this time more about the human mind than the machines.
A Life on Our Planet: My Witness Stateme: David Attenborough looks back on a lifetime of filming the natural world, sets out how much of it has gone, and then lays out how it could grow back. Close to the solarpunk world Vincent likes to dream about.
Chasing Shadows: Tom DeLonge, the Blink-182 guitarist turned UFO campaigner, co-wrote this thriller with A. J. Hartley: a marine pilot, an activist heiress, a sceptical podcaster and a boy in a 1939 Nazi camp all brush up against technology that shouldn’t exist.
What Doesn't Kill Us: How Freezing Water: Journalist Scott Carney sets out to debunk Wim Hof and ends up training with him instead: ice baths, odd breathing, and a climb up Kilimanjaro with hardly any clothes on.
Entangled Life: How Fungi Make Our World: Merlin Sheldrake goes underground to the fungi that link tree roots into vast networks, feed forests, turn minds and might yet clean up our mess. The beech woods he grew up by run on it.
In Plain Sight: An Australian investigative journalist goes through decades of UFO sightings, whistleblowers and Pentagon secrecy, and takes the question seriously. The telescope in the lamp room hasn’t turned anything up yet.
Animal Farm: The animals chase off Farmer Jones and run the farm themselves, until the pigs start walking on two legs. The sheep only bleat the slogans, which is a poor showing for the sheep.
The Paper Menagerie and Other Stories: Ken Liu’s short stories, from a boy whose mother folds paper animals that come to life to quiet, aching science fiction about memory and history.
Boeddhisme in alle eenvoud: Ontwaak en o: The Dutch translation of Steve Hagen’s Buddhism Plain and Simple: the Buddha’s teaching without the robes and incense, boiled down to seeing what’s actually in front of you, right now.
Hex: A town where a centuries-old witch with her eyes and mouth sewn shut walks the streets, and no one who lives there may ever leave. The Dutch original was set in Beek, near Nijmegen, not far from Arnhem.
The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle: Toru Okada’s cat goes missing, then his wife, and the search leads him down a dry well, into strange phone calls and back to a war in Manchuria. Charlie and George are advised not to wander off.
Possible Minds: 25 Ways of Looking at AI: John Brockman asks twenty-five scientists and thinkers to look at artificial intelligence again, starting from Norbert Wiener’s old warnings about machines.
Rebooting AI: Building Artificial Intell: Gary Marcus and Ernest Davis argue that deep learning, for all its tricks, lacks common sense and real understanding, and set out what a sturdier kind of AI would need.
Starsight: Spensa, the hot-headed pilot from Skyward, goes undercover among the aliens who keep her people trapped on their planet, with only her chatty AI ship M-Bot to help.
De schaduw van de wind: In post-war Barcelona a boy is taken to the Cemetery of Forgotten Books, picks a novel by Julián Carax, and finds that someone has been burning every other copy. A book about loving books, now on a shelf of its own.
Great Expectations: Pip, an orphan on the Kentish marshes, meets an escaped convict, a jilted bride who stopped all her clocks, and a mystery benefactor who makes him a gentleman.
Acid for the Children: Flea, the Red Hot Chili Peppers’ bassist, writes about growing up wild in 1970s Los Angeles, and stops just as the band begins. The other half of the story is on the same shelf, in Scar Tissue.
Sputnik Sweetheart: K is in love with his friend Sumire, a would-be novelist who falls for an older woman, Miu. Then Sumire vanishes from a small Greek island and K flies out to look for her. Murakami at his most wistful.
The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck: A C: Mark Manson’s blunt self-help: life is short, so pick carefully what you care about and stop chasing feeling good all the time. He gave it three stars, which is at least some.
Kafka on the Shore: A fifteen-year-old runs away from home and hides in a quiet private library, while an old man who can talk to cats sets off on a journey of his own. Fish fall from the sky.
Conscious: A Brief Guide to the Fundamen: A short, clear book asking what consciousness actually is, and whether it could go all the way down, even into things we don’t think of as minds at all.
Brief Answers to the Big Questions: Stephen Hawking’s last book takes on ten big ones, from whether there is a God to whether we can travel in time and whether AI will outsmart us.
The Three-Body Problem: It begins in the Cultural Revolution and ends with a reply from the stars: a scientist sends a signal, physicists start dying, and an odd virtual-reality game hints at a world with three suns. One of his favourite series starts here.
The Gene: An Intimate History: Siddhartha Mukherjee tells the story of the gene, from Mendel’s pea plants to editing DNA, woven together with his own family’s history of mental illness.
Het pauperparadijs: Suzanna Jansen traces her own family back to Veenhuizen in Drenthe, one of the nineteenth-century colonies where the Dutch poor were sent to be made into decent citizens, generation after generation.
The Restaurant at the End of the Univers: Arthur Dent, still in his dressing gown, ends up having dinner at Milliways, where the show each night is the end of the universe. One star fewer than the first book.
De geschiedenis van de vooruitgang: Rutger Bregman shows how much better life has become over the centuries, with longer, richer, safer lives for most people, and then asks why we still feel so uneasy about the future.
Utopia for Realists: How We Can Build th: Rutger Bregman makes the case for universal basic income, a shorter working week and open borders, with history and experiments to back him up.
The War on Normal People: The Truth Abou: Written before Andrew Yang ran for president: his case that automation is quietly emptying out ordinary American jobs, and that a universal basic income is the way through.
Mockingjay: The last of the Hunger Games, where Katniss is no longer in the arena but has become the face of a rebellion she isn’t sure she trusts.
Catching Fire: Katniss survived the arena and now has to keep up the act on a victory tour, while the districts start to stir and the Capitol plans something special for the next Games.
The Hunger Games: In a country that makes its children fight to the death on television, Katniss takes her little sister’s place in the arena.
The End of Faith: Religion, Terror, and: Written after 9/11, Sam Harris’s argument that religious faith shields dangerous beliefs from criticism, ending, a little unexpectedly, with a chapter on meditation and spirituality without dogma.
Norwegian Wood: Toru Watanabe hears a Beatles song on a plane and is carried back to his student years in late-sixties Tokyo, and to two very different young women. Murakami at his most down to earth, with no sheep, wild or otherwise.
A Crack in Creation: The New Power to Co: One of the scientists behind CRISPR explains how she helped find a way to edit DNA with startling precision, and what we ought to do now that we can.
Skyward: Spensa wants to fly fighters for her planet’s last outpost of humans, but her father was branded a coward. Then she finds a wrecked ship with a sarcastic AI that is mostly worried about mushrooms.
21 Lessons for the 21st Century: After the deep past and the far future, Yuval Noah Harari turns to now: fake news, nationalism, work in an age of algorithms. It ends, of all places, on meditation.
Oathbringer: The third Stormlight book, a real door-stopper, where Dalinar’s past finally catches up with him, Kaladin goes home and the Knights Radiant gather in a tower city high in the mountains.
Our Mathematical Universe: My Quest for: Physicist Max Tegmark argues that reality doesn’t just follow mathematics but is mathematics, taking in the Big Bang and several layers of multiverse along the way.
Edgedancer: Lift, a young thief with a strange power and an even stranger appetite, runs from the Azish capital to a city where someone is hunting people like her. Mostly she would like some pancakes.
Words of Radiance: Book two of the Stormlight Archive: Kaladin and his bridgemen, Shallan with her sketchbook and a talking pattern, and a war on the Shattered Plains, over a thousand pages of it.
The Way of Kings: On a storm-battered world, a slave carrying bridges into battle, a young scholar with a secret and a highprince haunted by visions all get pulled towards something bigger. The first Stormlight brick.
Barking Up the Wrong Tree: The Surprisin: Eric Barker rounds up studies and stories on what actually makes people successful: whether nice guys finish last, whether confidence matters, whether quitters ever win.
Life 3.0: Being Human in the Age of Arti: MIT physicist Max Tegmark on what happens when AI catches up with us and then keeps going, from jobs and weapons to the far future of life in the cosmos. It’s on the shelf twice.
Iron Gold: Ten years after the revolution, Darrow is still fighting, and the story widens to a refugee, a thief and an exiled prince who all have reasons to doubt him. Red Rising, grown up and messier.
Morning Star: The end of Darrow’s first trilogy, a Red miner disguised as a Gold, with his whole rebellion against the Society now on the line.
Golden Son: Darrow has made it inside the ruling Golds of Mars, and now has to survive their wars and politics while planning to bring the whole lot down.
Red Rising: Darrow digs helium-3 under the surface of Mars, believing he’s helping make the planet liveable, until he learns the truth and is rebuilt as a Gold to bring the ruling caste down from inside. The start of one of his favourite series.
Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind: How a fairly unremarkable ape took over the planet: Harari’s whistle-stop history from foragers to farming, money, empires and science, held together by the stories we all agree to believe in.
The Hero of Ages: The end of the first Mistborn trilogy, with ash falling, mists killing and Vin and Elend racing to understand what they let loose at the Well of Ascension.
Genghis Khan and the Making of the Moder: Weatherford makes the case that the Mongols were more than raiders, spreading trade, paper money, postal relays and religious tolerance from China to Hungary.
The Well of Ascension: The tyrant is dead and Vin and Elend have to actually run the city, with three armies at the gates and the mists turning strange.
Mistborn: The Final Empire: Ash falls from the sky, a god-emperor has ruled for a thousand years, and a street thief called Vin is pulled into a crew planning the most unlikely heist of all: bringing him down.
Homo Deus: A History of Tomorrow: Harari turns from the past to the future: with famine, plague and war largely tamed, humans may reach for immortality and godhood while data and algorithms quietly take charge.
Astrophysics for People in a Hurry: Neil deGrasse Tyson runs through the universe, from the Big Bang to dark matter, in short chapters meant for a commute. A good primer before an evening at the telescope in the lamp room.
I, Robot: Linked stories told by robot psychologist Susan Calvin, each one a puzzle about how robots bound by the Three Laws still manage to go wrong. Asimov had been thinking about AI safety since the 1940s.
Endurance: Shackleton's Incredible Voyag: Shackleton’s ship is crushed by Antarctic ice, and twenty-eight men spend over a year camping on floes and sailing a lifeboat across the worst sea on earth. It makes any wild camp in the Alps look comfortable.
Angels & Demons: Robert Langdon’s first outing: a stolen canister of antimatter is hidden somewhere in Vatican City during a papal conclave, and the clues run through Rome’s churches and an old secret society, the Illuminati.
The Evening and the Morning: The prequel to The Pillars of the Earth, set around the year 1000, when Kingsbridge is barely a village and a young boatbuilder, a Norman noblewoman and an ambitious monk try to survive Viking raids and local tyrants.
Consider Phlebas: Horza, a shapeshifter fighting for the Idirans against the Culture, is sent after a ship’s Mind hiding on a dead planet. Banks’s first trip into the Culture, seen from someone who hates it.
Light Bringer: Book six of Red Rising: Darrow is back from the brink and the war he started has spread across the whole solar system, with old friends and old enemies switching sides.
Dark Age: Ten years into the war against the Golds, Darrow is losing on Mercury while the new Republic falls apart behind him. The fifth Red Rising book, and a long one.
My Big Toe: Discovery (My Big Toe): Physicist Thomas Campbell, who worked on out-of-body research with Robert Monroe, begins his theory of everything, in which consciousness comes first and our physical world works rather like a simulation.
Dreamland: An Autobiography: Bob Lazar’s own account of the claim that made him famous: that in the late eighties he worked on reverse-engineering alien craft at a site called S-4, near Area 51.
How to Change Your Mind: The New Science: Michael Pollan looks into the history and new science of psilocybin and LSD, and then tries them himself, with the ego and consciousness under the microscope.
Dreaming Yourself Awake: Lucid Dreaming: A Buddhist teacher and scholar takes you from learning to notice you’re dreaming to the older Tibetan practice of meditating inside the dream itself. Close to the meditation retreat he loved, though this one happens in bed.
Hacking the Out of Body Experience: Leve: Robert Peterson, who has had out-of-body experiences since the 1970s, sets out practical methods for having one yourself, with the science around it. A how-to for one of Vincent’s favourite subjects.
Neuralink and the Brain’s Magical Future: Tim Urban’s enormous Wait But Why explainer, starting with jellyfish and ending at brain–computer interfaces and Elon Musk’s plan to link us to machines.
Zomerhuis met zwembad / Het diner: Two Herman Koch novels in one: The Dinner, where two brothers and their wives get through a very expensive meal while circling what their sons have done, and Summer House with Swimming Pool, about a GP and a holiday gone badly wrong.
The AI Revolution: The Road to Superinte: Tim Urban’s long Wait But Why essay on how AI could go from narrow to superintelligent faster than anyone’s intuition allows, stick figures and all.
The Elon Musk Blog Series: Wait But Why: Tim Urban’s long, stick-figure-filled posts from when Musk let him in: how Tesla and SpaceX work, why the rockets matter, and how Musk reasons from first principles.
Death's End: The last of the Three-Body books follows an aerospace engineer who keeps waking up in later and stranger centuries, as the stakes go from one planet to the whole universe.
The Dark Forest: Humanity has four centuries before an alien fleet arrives, and four people are handed near-unlimited resources to make secret plans to save it. One of them, a sociologist named Luo Ji, would much rather not.
Waking Up: A Guide to Spirituality Witho: Sam Harris makes the case that meditation can show you something true about the mind, without needing to believe anything religious, and that the self isn’t quite what it seems.
The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy: Arthur Dent’s house is about to be knocked down for a bypass, which turns out to be the least of his problems once Earth is cleared for a hyperspace one. Bring a towel.
Ready Player One: In a grim 2045, everyone escapes into a vast virtual world, and its dead creator has hidden a fortune in it behind puzzles from 1980s games and films. Light reading for a man building his own game.
Elon Musk: Tesla, SpaceX, and the Quest: Ashlee Vance follows Musk from a rough childhood in South Africa through PayPal to the years when Tesla and SpaceX both came close to going under.
The Martian: Astronaut Mark Watney is left for dead on Mars and has to science his way out, growing potatoes and swearing at every setback. Andy Weir later did it again with Project Hail Mary, which Vincent loves.
Dark Matter: A physics teacher is knocked out on the way home and wakes in a life where he never married his wife and became a famous scientist instead. Now he has to find his way back through all the other versions.
The Slow Regard of Silent Things: Seven days with Auri alone in the Underthing beneath the University, tidying, naming and making things right. Hardly any plot and no one else to talk to; Rothfuss himself warned some readers off.
The Wise Man's Fear: Kvothe goes on telling his life story: trouble at the University, a strange court, a fairy, and some hard lessons in fighting. Book three still hasn’t come out.
The Name of the Wind: Kvothe, now an innkeeper hiding under another name, tells a chronicler the true story of his life: travelling players, years on the streets and the University where he learns real magic. One of his favourites.
The Ultimate Hitchhiker’s Guide to the G: All five Hitchhiker’s books in one: Arthur Dent loses his house and his planet on the same Thursday and gets towed round the galaxy in his dressing gown.
Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strat: Nick Bostrom asks what happens when we build a mind that is smarter than us, and how on earth we would keep it on our side.
The Kaleidoscope: The Gift of Madness: A short indie sci-fi novel set in a future where androids, the first life after humanity, arrive as unwelcome immigrants, and have to ask whether the oppressed can ever forgive the ones who made them.
Scar Tissue: Anthony Kiedis tells the Red Hot Chili Peppers story from the inside, with the songs, the women and a long, honest fight with heroin.
The Winds of Winter: The sixth Song of Ice and Fire book, which George R.R. Martin still hasn’t finished. He gave it five stars anyway.
A Dance with Dragons: The fifth book of A Song of Ice and Fire: Daenerys struggles to rule a city, Jon Snow holds the Wall, and Tyrion is on the run.
A Feast for Crows: After the war, Westeros counts its dead, and the story follows Cersei, Jaime, Brienne, Sam and Arya while half the cast waits for the next book. He’s still waiting for one too.
A Storm of Swords: The third Song of Ice and Fire book: the War of the Five Kings grinds on, Jon goes beyond the Wall and Daenerys buys an army.
A Clash of Kings: Five men call themselves king of Westeros at once, and the war spreads, while beyond the Wall and across the sea other things start to stir. He gave it five stars, and also a book that doesn’t exist yet.
A Game of Thrones: Lord Eddard Stark rides south to serve his old friend the king and finds a court full of knives, while beyond the Wall winter is coming.
Zomerhuis met zwembad: Marc Schlosser is a GP whose famous actor patient has just died, and the story keeps returning to the summer holiday their two families spent together at a villa by the sea. Herman Koch at his most uncomfortable.
The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo: A disgraced journalist is hired to find out what happened to a girl who vanished from a wealthy Swedish family’s island in 1966, and teams up with Lisbeth Salander, a brilliant hacker.
Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: No Hogwarts this year: Harry, Ron and Hermione are on the run, camping in the woods and hunting for the pieces of Voldemort’s soul.
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban: A man escapes the wizard prison everyone said was escape-proof, and he seems to be coming for Harry. The one with the Dementors, the Marauder’s Map and Buckbeak.
Wizard's First Rule: Richard Cypher is a woods guide until he rescues a mysterious woman, Kahlan, and is named the Seeker of Truth, the one who has to stop the tyrant Darken Rahl. The first of a very long series.
Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone: A boy who lives in a cupboard under the stairs learns on his eleventh birthday that he’s a wizard, and is whisked off to Hogwarts.
Fight Club: An insomniac office worker meets Tyler Durden, a soap salesman with big ideas, and together they start a club in a basement. The first rule is well known.
Brave New World: A future where babies come off a production line, everyone is happy because they’re told to be, and there’s always soma. Then a man raised outside it all comes to visit.
Joe Speedboot: Fransje, who can’t walk or speak after an accident, watches his village on the Rhine and the boy Joe Speedboot, who builds bombs and aeroplanes and plans to leave. Fransje happens to be very good at arm-wrestling.
The Hobbit, or There and Back Again: Bilbo Baggins is perfectly happy in his hole until a wizard and thirteen dwarves turn up for tea and take him off to steal back a dragon’s gold. A walking holiday that gets badly out of hand.
The Girl Who Played with Fire: Lisbeth Salander is suddenly wanted for murder when two people working on a Millennium exposé are shot, and Mikael Blomkvist sets out to prove she didn’t do it.
The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet’s Nest: Lisbeth Salander wakes up in hospital with a bullet wound to the head and a murder trial ahead, while Blomkvist goes after the secret group in the security service that wants her silenced.
The Lost Symbol: Robert Langdon is called to Washington, D.C., where a severed hand in the Capitol starts a night of Freemason secrets, while a scientist works on whether thought can change the physical world.
The Da Vinci Code: A curator is found dead in the Louvre, laid out like a Leonardo drawing, and a Harvard professor of symbols has to work out why, on the run across Paris and London.
The Return of the King: The end of The Lord of the Rings: the siege of Minas Tirith, the last miles across Mordor and the long road home to the Shire, which turns out not to be quite as they left it.
The Fellowship of the Ring: Frodo inherits a ring that must never be used and sets out from the Shire to get rid of it. Mostly a very long walk, which someone who has done the Tour du Mont Blanc can appreciate.
The Two Towers: The Fellowship breaks apart: Aragorn, Legolas and Gimli run across Rohan towards Helm’s Deep and the Ents, while Frodo and Sam walk to Mordor with Gollum as their guide.
1984: Winston Smith rewrites old newspapers at the Ministry of Truth and starts, very quietly, to keep a diary. Big Brother is watching.
Circe: Circe, a nymph born among the Greek gods, is banished to an island, where over long centuries she learns herbs and witchcraft and has visitors, Odysseus among them. It’s lying open on his desk, because he’s reading it now.
